assertion: The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) reported that in October 2026, it estimated the federal government incurred a deficit of $409 billion... This is $125 billion more than the shortfall recorded last October.
warehouse_value: Treasury MTS Oct 2026: receipts $368.9B, outlays $773.0B, deficit $404.1B; Oct 2025 deficit $284.3B (+$119.8B). CBO's $409B/+$125B matches.
sql: SELECT record_date,line_code_nbr,current_month_rcpt_outly_amt FROM econ.mts_outlays_by_function WHERE line_code_nbr IN ('120','340') AND record_date IN ('2025-10-31','2026-10-31')
independent_value: Search summary of CBO MBR: $409B, ~$778B spending, $369B revenue, +$125B
reason: Early estimate; matches the figure CBO published.

sources.title: CBO MBR summary (403 on direct fetch)

assertion: Revenues were $36 billion lower, and outlays were $89 billion higher than the same month last year, according to the CBO.
reason: Matches CBO's early figures; MTS agrees within a few billion.

assertion: The deficit of $409 billion was more than $100 billion a week.
inaccuracy: The claim says more than $100B per week; the data says October has 31 days (4.43 weeks), so $409B is about $92B per week. Only a four-week month gives $102B.

assertion: The report suggested October's federal deficit was that much higher due to shifts in the timing of certain federal payments that otherwise would have been made on November 1 (that date fell on a weekend in 2025 and 2026, therefore pushing those payments into October of each year).
inaccuracy: The claim says timing shifts made October's deficit that much higher than last year; the evidence says the shift hit both Octobers (Nov 1 was a Saturday in 2025 and a Sunday in 2026), so it cancels out and cannot account for the $125B year-over-year increase.
warehouse_value: Net interest alone rose $12B (90.9B to 103.1B) between the two Octobers.
source_finding: Treasury MTS shows both Octobers carried the weekend-date shift.

assertion: In its budget review, the CBO showed that for the fiscal year of 2026, the deficit was at 6.2% of the nation's GDP, up from 5.8% a year prior. This percentage is greater than the 50-year average of 3.8%, and has only previously been matched or exceeded eight times since 1946: from 2009 through 2012 and in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.
reason: Percentages not found in any copy I could open; magnitude plausible ($2.0T deficit vs roughly $32T GDP). The count of eight matches the years listed.
searched: CBO Monthly Budget Review October 2026 deficit 6.2 percent of GDP

assertion: The total deficit for the year was $1.9 trillion, the CBO added.
inaccuracy: The claim says $1.9 trillion; the evidence says $2.0 trillion (receipts $5.403T minus outlays $7.396T = $1.99T). The $1.9T is the earlier baseline figure CBO's result exceeded by $140B.
why_not: The $1.9T in the AAF source is the earlier baseline, not the actual result, so it confirms rather than changes the grade.
sql: SELECT current_fytd_rcpt_outly_amt FROM econ.mts_outlays_by_function WHERE record_date='2026-09-30' AND line_code_nbr IN ('120','340')
independent_value: AAF quoting CBO: $2.0T actual vs $1.9T baseline

assertion: Government income was up for the year to $5.4 trillion, up $169 billion in the 2025 fiscal year, thanks, in large part, to increases in collections of individual income and payroll taxes.
Total outlays increased by $217 billion—most of which came from an uptick in Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid.
inaccuracy: The claim says outlays rose $217 billion; the data says outlays rose $386 billion (to $7.4T), while $217-218 billion is the rise in the deficit.

assertion: $1.14 trillion spent on interest on the public debt.
reason: MTS net interest FY2026 is $1.052T; $1.14T may be a gross-interest definition but I could not open CBO's text.
measure: federal budget deficit monthly receipts outlays interest on public debt
searched: CBO October 2026 monthly budget review interest on public debt

assertion: Bessent described this summer's actions as a "Treasury twist."
inaccuracy: The claim says Bessent used the term; the CNBC transcript shows host Sara Eisen used it in her question ("what I would call a Treasury twist").
independent_value: CNBC transcript: 'twist' occurs once, in the interviewer's question

assertion: JPMorgan's co-head of global fundamental research, James Sullivan, described it as "paying your mortgage with your credit card. It can work for a while, but eventually the mismatch starts to become more obvious."
speaker: James Sullivan
independent_value: CNBC: 'a little bit like paying your mortgage with your credit card...'

assertion: A range of factors have brought down longer-dated yields and smoothed volatility.
inaccuracy: The claim says longer-dated yields came down; the data says the 30-year averaged 5.22% in Aug, 5.37% Sep, 5.47% Oct, 5.30% Nov-to-date: below October's peak but above August and July (5.10%).
warehouse_value: DGS30 monthly avg: Jul 5.10, Aug 5.22, Sep 5.37, Oct 5.47, Nov 5.30
sql: SELECT substr(CAST("date" AS VARCHAR),1,7) m, avg("value") FROM econ.fred_indicators WHERE series='DGS30' AND "date">='2026-07-01' GROUP BY 1
